title: Why Are My Hardwood Floors Turning Gray or Black? Causes and the Fix
meta: Gray hardwood means worn finish letting water into bare wood; black is water or urine reacting with tannins. Wills Flooring explains the fix in Seattle homes.
keywords: hardwood floors turning gray, black spots on hardwood floors, gray hardwood floor near door, black stains hardwood floor water, can gray hardwood be refinished, hardwood floor refinishing Seattle

blocks.lead: Gray means the finish has worn through and water is getting into bare wood; black means water or pet urine has reacted with the tannins in the wood, or mold has set in. Gray sands out with a full refinish; black often needs bleaching, board replacement or a dark stain.
blocks.detail: Neither one is fixable with a screen-and-recoat, because the problem is in the wood, not the finish. The good news is that gray floors are one of the most satisfying refinishes we do. The wood underneath is usually perfect.

blocks.html: Seattle floors go gray for a very Seattle reason: eight months of wet shoes coming through the front door onto a finish that was last redone when the house sold. A Ballard bungalow with 1925 oak, a Wallingford Tudor with fir, a Beacon Hill rambler with 1950s red oak: we see the same gray fan shape spreading from the entry, the same dark ring under the dog bowl, and the same black halo around the dishwasher. This post explains what each color tells you, how to test it yourself, and what the fix costs at our published rates.

blocks.text: What the color is telling you

items.title: Gray: bare wood taking on water
items.text: Polyurethane wears thinnest where feet land. Once it is gone, every wet footprint soaks into the wood, the surface fibers swell and oxidize, and the boards turn a dull silver-gray. Run your hand over it: gray wood feels slightly rough. It is cosmetic, and it sands out.

items.title: Black: iron and tannin
items.text: Oak and fir are full of tannins. When water carries iron to them, from a nail, an old radiator leg, a steel dog bowl or the salts in pet urine, the reaction makes iron tannate, the same black as old ink. It goes deeper than gray and does not always sand out.

items.title: Black and fuzzy: mold or mildew
items.text: Long-term moisture from a leak, a planter or a damp basement grows dark mold in and under the boards. It smells musty and the wood may be soft. This one needs the source fixed and often board replacement, not just sanding.

items.title: Gray near south windows: UV
items.text: Old-growth fir in Queen Anne and Wallingford houses bleaches gray under sun through a bare window, especially under a rug edge where the contrast shows. This is finish and surface fiber only, and it sands out completely.

blocks.text: Test it yourself in two minutes

items.html: The water drop test. Put a single drop of water on the gray area. If it soaks in and darkens the wood within a minute, the finish is gone and you are looking at bare wood. If it beads up, the finish is intact and the gray is something else, probably dirt or a failed wax layer.

Rub a black spot with a damp white cloth. If nothing transfers and the spot stays put, it is in the wood (tannin or mold). If black comes off, it is surface grime or mildew on top of the finish and a good cleaning may fix it.
Press the black area with a screwdriver. If the wood is firm, it can be sanded and treated. If it is soft or spongy, the board is rotting and needs to be replaced.

blocks.text: How we fix it, step by step

items.text: Moisture meter on the dark boards, a look at the source (door, appliance, plumbing, crawlspace), and a probe for soft wood. You get a firm written quote with any board replacement listed.
Full sanding to bare wood. Gray disappears in the first pass because it is only the top few thousandths of an inch. Black spots either lighten to a shadow or stay, which tells us how deep they go.

Oxalic acid wood bleach on remaining iron-tannin marks, neutralized and dried. Most spots fade to a faint shadow. Anything that stays black is cut out and replaced with matching oak or fir, then sanded flush.
Three coats of Bona water-based finish for a natural floor at $3.99 per sq ft. If shadows remain and you want them gone, a medium or dark stain at $6.50 per sq ft hides what bleach could not.

blocks.text: Refinish or replace? Where the line is

a.title: Sanding is the right call when
items: The gray is on the surface and the water drop test confirms bare wood
Black spots are small, firm and few
The wood is at least 3/32 in above the tongue and has not been sanded four times already

b.title: Sanding alone will not do it when
items: Boards are soft, spongy or smell musty
Black covers a large area under a leak and goes through the board
Boards are cupped or buckled from standing water

blocks.title: Fix the water before you fix the floor:
blocks.text: A gray entry will go gray again if the door still leaks and the mat is still missing. A black halo around the dishwasher will come back if the supply line still drips. We will tell you at the estimate if the floor is fighting a water problem we cannot fix, and we would rather you spend that money on the plumber first.
Keeping a Seattle floor from going gray again

items: A real doormat outside and a washable rug inside the front door, both without rubber backing on a new finish.
Shoes off at the entry from October to May. Most of the gray we sand out is winter rain.
A screen-and-recoat at $1.99 per sq ft every 4 to 6 years in the traffic lanes, before the finish wears through. Once it is gray, the recoat option is gone.
A silicone tray under the pet bowls and a drip pan under the fridge.

blocks.html: If the dark spots are from a pet rather than water, the chemistry and the odds are different. See our post on whether pet urine stains can be sanded out.

faq.q: Can gray hardwood floors be refinished?
faq.a: Yes, and it is one of the most reliable refinishes there is. Gray is bare, weathered wood only a few thousandths of an inch deep. A full sanding removes it completely, and three coats of finish at $3.99 per sq ft leave the boards looking like new oak or fir. A recoat cannot fix gray because the finish is already gone.

faq.q: Will black water stains come out of hardwood floors?
faq.a: Often, but not always. Sanding lightens most black marks, and oxalic acid wood bleach fades iron-tannin stains further. Spots that go through the board are cut out and replaced with matching wood. If faint shadows remain and bother you, a medium to dark stain at $6.50 per sq ft hides them.

faq.q: Why does my floor turn gray only near the front door?
faq.a: Because that is where the finish wears through first and where the water is. In Seattle that means eight or nine months of wet shoes landing on the same two square feet. Once the polyurethane is gone, every wet footprint soaks in, the fibers oxidize, and the wood turns silver-gray in a fan shape from the threshold.

faq.q: Is a gray or black floor a sign of mold?
faq.a: Gray almost never is; it is dry, weathered wood. Black can be either an iron-tannin reaction, which is harmless chemistry, or mold from ongoing moisture. Mold is usually fuzzy, smells musty and the wood may be soft. If it smells, find the water source before refinishing anything.

faq.q: Can I just recoat a gray floor instead of sanding it?
faq.a: No. A screen-and-recoat at $1.99 per sq ft only works when the old finish is intact, because it bonds a new coat to the old one. Gray wood has no finish left, and a recoat over it locks the gray in permanently under clear finish. Full sanding is the only fix once wood is gray.

faq.q: How much does it cost to fix gray floors in a Seattle house?
faq.a: At Wills Flooring's published rate, a natural sand and refinish is $3.99 per sq ft with a 500 sq ft minimum. A typical 700 sq ft Ballard main floor is 700 × $3.99 = $2,793. Spot bleaching and board replacement for black stains are quoted at the free estimate after we see them.
